1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Springer further demonstrated that these characteristics are both necessary and sufficient for defining the conjugacy classes within Sp_n(K). This research ultimately extends the earlier findings of Emil Artin, who had discovered similar classifications for the special linear group, but with an important distinction: the characteristic of the field K is no longer a limiting factor. Additionally, Springer's work on the symplectic group also presents a notable contrast to his own earlier findings, as well as those of others, demonstrating that the characteristic of the field K does, in fact, play a significant role in determining conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K). Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. It reveals that the relationship between collections of physical observables and associated physical states embodies the classical duality between actions and symmetries. This interpretation can be extended to more complex situations, offering a broader, more rigorous framework for understanding the physical implications of similar abstract relationships in quantum physics. It also highlights the limitations of the current formulation, suggesting that a more comprehensive analysis of states may require more intricate mathematical structures, such as modular tensor categories. These structures potentially contain the information necessary for defining topological quantum field theories, which could provide a more direct physical interpretation of the relationship between collections of physical observables and associated physical states. It further implies that certain abstract relationships, when embedded within the context of modular invariance, may give rise to physically meaningful concepts, linking the relationship between collections of physical observables and associated physical states to topological quantum field theories and their boundary modes that act as symmetries in (fractal) spacetime.

high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.  The model was further assessed for credibility and it was found to comply with observations from other areas, but it requires further validation.  The study also examined the possibility of accounting for gamma-rays with cosmic particles that have undergone acceleration and it was found that such a scenario is unlikely. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. As a result, it demonstrates that both problems are not only solvable but also characterized by the property of being able to establish a Euclidean embedding that preserves distances. Consequently, this indicates that both problems are capable of being defined in the context of the property of betweenness, which, in turn, implies that they are equivalent to each other. Furthermore, the article establishes that both problems are capable of being formulated in the context of the relation of interval, which, in turn, enables it to be compared to the traditional relation of the interval as defined by the real numbers. As a key contribution, the article formulates and proves the 'Interval Problem' for the specific type of metric spaces known as the metric tree, which, to this point, lacked a settled status. where the attractiveness of an approach lane, i.e., the length of its service

Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). Nevertheless, increasing the foot size beyond this point led to the feedback controller failing to prevent the robot from sinking into the ground. Finally, the height that the robot jumped to after adapting to its new environment was used as an indicator of its stability, and it was found that this height was significantly greater than that achieved with the feedforward control system

a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Our optimizations focus on applying modern programming techniques to enhance code efficiency and a customized interpreter designed to streamline text-based game simulations. 
We openly provide the modified source code of three game challenges, along with a level editor capable of converting existing TextWorld levels into a faster, newer format. 
Furthermore, we introduce a new benchmark focused on evaluating the practical efficiency of text-based game environments at a deeper level, encompassing various aspects like memory management, data structures, and computational operations. 
Our findings reveal that the speed of text-based game environments has a significant, critically impactful effect on extensive, prolonged testing, essentially making existing games too slow for widespread, widespread use. 
Finally, we successfully train multiple state-of-the-art agents on the original, slower versions of the three game challenges and our newly introduced benchmark, along with a newly introduced simpler companion benchmark, and compare their performance with the optimized, faster versions,

Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. Moreover, this research can be adapted to study the Galois group of randomly selected polynomials rather than generic ones. Through the study of these polynomial ensembles, we demonstrate the high probability of their Galois groups being maximally transitive, meaning their action on the underlying field's elements is unfettered for almost all polynomials. This phenomenon is contrasted with the behavior of individual polynomials, where only a minuscule subset exhibits this property.

To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. Experimental analysis using this new resource demonstrates the superiority of predicted indicators over traditional categories in describing the relationships between sentences, as measured by a cosine similarity score. This novel dataset is deemed an upgraded assessment of the already existing semantically annotated datasets. The data, along with processing instructions, can be obtained at this link: https://github.com/DiscPrompt/DiscSense. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. Another important factor it seems is the model's need for a feature representing the city's economic and residential zones. When these conditions are met, the model successfully forecasts the spread of riots, including the previously unsimulated Santiago scenario. Furthermore, it highlights the crucial role of a hitherto unquantified parameter, "social fatigue," in influencing the extent of unrest. Nevertheless, the project also emphasizes the complexity of Chile's unrest, stressing that the model's primary purpose is to demonstrate the feasibility of its approach, rather than offering a comprehensive explanation of the events it simulates. Ultimately, the project succeeds in adapting the epidemiological model for Santiago but reveals the need for a more nuanced representation of urban disorder that takes into account the diverse experiences of different community members. , we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Moreover, we demonstrate that the coefficient of the neutrino oscillation length, in the "solar" domain, is substantially smaller than the "atmospheric" scale, thereby justifying the neutralization of the matter term during solar neutrino evolution. Lastly, we validate the applicability of the linearized seesaw formula across all neutrino mass scales. In the simplest scoto-seesaw model, the dark matter is composed of two fermion pairs per unit of the "atmospheric" neutrino mass scale. Consequently, the dark matter annihilation cross-section is kept relatively high, resulting in an observable rate for the $\bar{\nu}\nu$ final state in dark matter detectors.

application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. This research was also highlighted in a Forbes magazine article as one of the top AI healthcare innovations in 2020. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/songdesong/StyleCXR, while our project video can be viewed on YouTube at https://youtube.com/medicalimagingneurips. Although our dataset-specific model is not intended for practical medical usage, it serves as a reliable benchmark for evaluating medical GAN-based applications. To further advance this research, we created the first-ever chest X-ray translation inference challenge, CNX-RITIC, which can be found on Alibaba's AI Challenge Platform
